value: tympanal-ridge motion peaked at 9.4 kHz in the individual shown, inside the male calling-song band (sound sweep 1 to 30 kHz at 66 dB SPL)
eye: tympanal ear (tympanal membrane, ridge and apodeme; mechanical response, not a neural threshold)
method: microscanning laser Doppler vibrometry of the tympanal ridge (TR) and apodeme (TA) of the intact ear, driven by a frequency-modulated sweep
conditions: female Cicadatra atra caught in July 2007; eight animals, one ear each; sweep 80 ms from 1 to 30 kHz, loudspeaker 0.25 m from the cicada, level held at 66 dB SPL across the range; no electrophysiological recording made at the same time; animals not anaesthetised, fixed to a brass bar with Blu-Tack, tested at 24 to 26 C

source.authors: Windmill JFC, Sueur J, Robert D
source.title: The next step in cicada audition: measuring pico-mechanics in the cicada's ear

quote: In this individual the maximal motion of the transect occurs at 9.4kHz, within the male calling song frequency band.
note: The 9.4 kHz peak is stated for the one individual shown in the figure, not as a best frequency across animals; the Discussion gives no best-tuning frequency for the ridge across animals and no hearing threshold. value: significantly fewer escape responses to 30 kHz pulse trains at 40 and 50 dB SPL than at 100 dB SPL
units: dB SPL (sound level at which escape responses fall off)
method: tethered flying moths played 2 s trains of 30 kHz pure-tone pulses modelled on search, approach and terminal phases of big brown bat calls, from 40 to 100 dB SPL; escape responses scored from infrared video
conditions: laboratory-reared virgin moths 2 to 3 days old (Methods list 49 males and 47 females; per-level sample sizes are printed only beneath the sound levels in Figure 3 and were not read); moth tied by a nylon line around the neck, electrostatic speaker 20 cm away; stimuli in random order, different stimuli to the same moth about 20 min apart, so each moth was tested repeatedly; 30 kHz was chosen for simplicity, not as a best frequency

source.title: Early erratic flight response of the lucerne moth to the quiet echolocation calls of distant bats

quote: However, stimuli that were presented at 40 and 50 dB SPL induced significantly fewer escape responses than those presented at 100 dB SPL (χ²₁ > 32.16, adjusted P < 0.0001) (Fig 4A).
note: Behavioural finding, not an auditory threshold or audiogram. The preceding Results sentence gives pooled escape rates of 91% at 100 dB SPL against 22% at 40, 53% at 50, 82% at 60, 80% at 70, 85% at 80 and 83% at 90 dB SPL; overall evasive actions (turning away plus erratic responses) at 60, 70, 80 and 90 dB SPL did not differ significantly from 100 dB SPL. The paper gives the moth ears as sensitive to 30 to 100 kHz and cites an earlier study for auditory-cell thresholds of about 48 to 53 dB SPL; it gives no best frequency. Crossref confirmed authors, volume and issue (WebFetch).

value: auditory brainstem response audiogram with two regions of best sensitivity, centred near 1.2 kHz (0.875 to 1.5 kHz) and 2.6 kHz (2.2 to 3.0 kHz); thresholds in the lower region 61 to 63 dB
eye: inner ear, amphibian and basilar papillae (recorded as auditory brainstem response)
method: auditory brainstem response to tone bursts and clicks with subdermal needle electrodes; thresholds detected by eye
conditions: 35 adult frogs (17 females, 18 males), one recording session of about 1.5 h per frog; immobilised with d-tubocurarine, topical lidocaine; body temperature 17.0 to 20.0 C; frog 30 cm from a speaker in a sound-attenuating chamber (below about 1.1 kHz that distance is under one wavelength, so particle motion could contribute); the paper names the species Hyla chrysoscelis

source.authors: Schrode KM, Buerkle NP, Brittan-Powell EF, Bee MA
source.title: Auditory brainstem responses in Cope's gray treefrog (Hyla chrysoscelis): effects of frequency, level, sex and size

quote: One region of best sensitivity was broadly centered around 1.2 kHz (between 0.875 and 1.5 kHz), and a second was centered around 2.6 kHz (between 2.2 and 3.0 kHz).
note: The quote gives the two sensitivity regions; the 61 to 63 dB figure is from the next Results sentence, which adds that these lower-region thresholds were generally 2.5 to 4.4 dB higher than those of the higher region, and that thresholds at 1.5 to 2.0 kHz were about 5 to 8 dB above the most sensitive frequencies. The authors say ABR thresholds were on average 15 to 25 dB higher than midbrain-recording thresholds (an earlier study of a different population), and that sex and size had no effect on ABR thresholds. Species filed under the accepted name Dryophytes chrysoscelis (GBIF ACCEPTED; Hylidae). Authors, volume and pages from Crossref (WebFetch).

source.title: Sensitivity of Pagurus bernhardus (L.) to substrate-borne vibration and anthropogenic noise
source.journal: Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology 474: 185-194

value: antenna-movement threshold averaged 0.11 to 0.29 m/s2 RMS across frequencies (flat curve), most sensitive at 90 Hz
method: staircase method with substrate vibration from an electromagnetic shaker; indicator 1 was a clear movement of the second antenna at signal onset or during the signal
conditions: common hermit crabs in Littorina shells collected from the Scarborough shore, held at about 11 to 12 C on a 12:12 light cycle, starved 24 to 48 h, acclimated 24 to 48 h; 8 s sine waves with 1 s rise and decay at seven frequencies from 5 to 410 Hz, amplitude changed in 6 dB steps; threshold taken as the mean of two alternating plateau amplitudes over 10 presentations; one crab tested per day, frequencies in random order 10 to 20 min apart; 45 crabs in total, each used once apart from the re-test experiments; indicator 1 used on 35 crabs
quote: An approximately flat response curve was obtained for indicator 1 with average sensitivities between 0.11 – 0.29 m s-2 (n = 35, RMS, vertical axis) and greatest sensitivity at 90 Hz.
note: Range of averages across the seven test frequencies, not a single threshold. The authors say the stimulus may also have produced water-borne particle motion, that laboratory conditions cannot fully replicate the seabed, and that they cannot say to which of the three axes the crabs were sensitive. Crabs held for weeks in the laboratory were less sensitive; the Abstract gives down to 0.02 m/s2 RMS for crabs tested soonest after capture. Accepted manuscript on the Hull repository (free copy); Crossref confirmed authors, volume, pages.

quote: On average, across all specimens, both tympanal membranes showed best response at 23.63 kHz ± 4.06 kHz, n = 42 (figure 3a,b).
note: Tuning of the eardrum, with no hearing threshold in dB SPL and no neural or behavioural recording. Females 22.92 and males 24.41 kHz (n = 22 and 20 membranes); the sex difference was not significant (p = 0.055), and anterior and posterior membranes did not differ (p = 0.43).
